task: Write a blog post for the school website, for students aged 13-15, about a place in your city that you recommend for a weekend visit. Describe it, explain why you like it and give some advice to visitors.
text:
My Favourite Escape: Why You Should Visit the Old Harbour This Weekend

Have you ever felt that your weekends disappear before you notice them? Between homework, football practice and family visits, I used to feel exactly like that, until my cousin took me to the Old Harbour in our city. Since then it has become my favourite place to relax, and I would like to share it with you.

The Old Harbour is only twenty minutes from the school by bus, and the ticket costs less than two euros. When you arrive, the first thing you notice is the smell of fresh bread and salt water. There are small fishing boats painted in blue and yellow, and old warehouses that have been changed into cafés, galleries and a tiny museum. In my opinion, the best part is the long stone pier. If you walk to the end of it in the late afternoon, you can watch the sun go down behind the cranes while the seagulls argue over the fishermen's leftovers.

There is something for everyone. If you are interested in history, the museum shows photographs of how the harbour looked a hundred years ago, and the entrance is free for students. If you prefer food, I strongly recommend the bakery called Maria's, where a warm cinnamon roll costs one euro fifty. And if you like being active, you can rent a bicycle and follow the path along the water for six kilometres.

However, the harbour is not perfect. On Saturdays it gets very crowded, so it is much more pleasant to go on Sunday morning, when it is quiet and the light is beautiful for photos. Also, the wind can be surprisingly cold, even in spring, so bring a jacket. Another thing I would suggest is to take a bag with you, because the seagulls are not shy and will steal your snack if you leave it open!

What I like most about the Old Harbour is that it makes me slow down. In a world where we are always looking at our phones, it is refreshing to sit on a bench and just listen to the boats moving on the water. After a stressful week of tests, an afternoon there makes me feel calm and ready for Monday.

So, if you are looking for a plan for this weekend, why not try it? Take a friend, bring some money for a cinnamon roll, and leave your worries at the bus stop. I promise you will not regret it. Let me know in the comments what you think, or send me a photo of your favourite spot!

task: Write a blog post for the school website, for students aged 13-15, about a place in your city that you recommend for a weekend visit. Describe it, explain why you like it and give some advice to visitors.
text:
A Great Place to Visit: The City Park

Hello everyone! Today I want to write about the City Park, because it is one of the best places in our city for the weekend and many students don't know it very well.

The park is in the center of the city, near the big train station. You can go there by bus number 12 or by bike. It is a very big park and it has a lake, a playground, a small zoo and many trees. In the summer I go there with my friends every Saturday. We usually bring some sandwiches and we play football on the grass. Sometimes we rent a boat on the lake, it costs five euros for one hour and it is really funny.

I like the park because it is quiet and you can relax there after school. Also, it is good for your health because you can run or walk and breathe the fresh air. My mother says that nature makes people happier, and I think she is right. When I am stressed about exams, I go to the park and I feel better. Last week, for example, I sat under a big tree with my book for two hours and I forgot all my problems.

If you want to visit the park, I have some advice for you. First, go in the morning because in the afternoon there are too many people. Second, don't forget to bring water, because the shops inside the park are very expensive. Third, be careful with the ducks, they can be aggressive when you give them bread!

In conclusion, the City Park is a wonderful place for everyone, for families, for students and for people who like animals. I recommend that you go there this weekend and tell me if you liked it. See you there!

task: Students read the magazine article 'The Girl Who Fixes Things'. It tells how Lena Brandt, 16, started a monthly 'repair café' in her town library after noticing that neighbours threw away toasters, radios and phones that were only slightly broken. The article opens with a description of her late grandfather's workshop (the smell of oil, shelves of old radios); he was a retired radio mechanic who taught her to solder when she was nine. In the first year volunteers repaired 312 items and the town council says almost two tonnes of waste stayed out of landfill. Mr Okafor, 78, is quoted: 'It's like getting an old friend back.' Lena is quoted: 'Throwing things away is easy. Learning how things work is the real power.' The writer uses phrases such as 'the throwaway habit' and 'disposable culture' and ends with a tips box. Questions: (1) What made Lena start the repair café? (2) Why does the writer begin with the grandfather's workshop? (3) How do the quotations and statistics help the writer persuade the reader? (4) What is the writer's attitude to throwing things away? Support your answer with words from the text. (5) Could a similar project work in your community? Explain, using ideas from the article.
text:
1. Lena started the repair café because she noticed that her neighbours were throwing away things that were only slightly broken, such as toasters, radios and phones, which could easily have been fixed. She also had the skills to do something about it, because she had learned to solder from her grandfather, so she decided to use them for her community.

2. I think the writer begins with the grandfather's workshop because it explains where Lena's talent and her values come from. It is not directly stated that he influenced her attitude, but the detailed description of the smell of oil and the shelves of old radios suggests that she grew up believing that objects deserve a second chance. It also makes the reader feel warmth towards Lena before they learn about her project, so the article reads like a personal story and not just a news report.

3. The quotation from Mr Okafor, "like getting an old friend back", adds an emotional, human voice and shows the real effect of the café on one person. The statistics, 312 items repaired and almost two tonnes of waste saved, give objective evidence that the project works on a large scale. Together they appeal both to feelings and to logic. The fact that the figure comes from the town council makes it more trustworthy than if Lena had simply claimed it herself.

4. The writer is critical of throwing things away. Phrases such as "the throwaway habit" and "disposable culture" have negative connotations and suggest that the behaviour is careless and unthinking, while Lena's work is described as "quiet" and brave. The writer therefore wants readers to feel that repairing is more admirable than replacing.

5. I think a similar project could work in my community, because at my school many students throw away headphones and chargers as soon as they stop working. Like in the article, there are probably older people with technical skills, for example my neighbour who repairs bicycles. However, unlike Lena's small town, my city is big, so it might be hard to find a free room, and we could start in the school library first. This would also connect with Lena's idea that learning how things work is a kind of power, because students would learn practical skills as well as save money.

task: Write an email to a penfriend from another country telling them about your school and what you do after school.
text:
Dear Tom,

How are you? I am fine. I hope you are fine too. I am writing you this email because I want to tell you about my school and about what I do after school. I will tell you about my school first and then I will tell you about what I do after school.

My school is a big school. My school is in the center of my city. My school have many students. There is one thousand students in my school. The students in my school are from many different places. My school is very good school and I like my school. My school have a big garden and a big library and a big sport hall.

My teachers are good. My English teacher is Mrs Lopez. Mrs Lopez is very nice teacher. She is a good teacher and she help us. My math teacher is Mr Chen. Mr Chen is a good teacher too but he give a lot of homeworks. I do not like homework but I do the homework. My favorite subject is English because English is a nice subject and I like English. I also like art because art is fun. I do not like physics because physics is difficult for me. Physics is very difficult and I do not understand physics.

At school we start at eight o'clock. We start at eight o'clock and we finish at three o'clock. At school we have lessons. We have six lessons every day. Every lesson is fifty minutes. After two lessons we have a break. In the break I talk with my friends. My friends are nice. My best friend is Ali. Ali is my best friend and he is in my class. We talk in the break and we eat in the break. We eat sandwiches in the break.

After school I go home. I go home by bus. The bus is very full. The bus is full and I stand in the bus. When I arrive at home I eat lunch. I eat lunch with my mother. My mother cook very good food. My mother is a good cook and I like her food. After lunch I do my homework. Homework is boring but I must do my homework. After I do my homework I am tired.

After the homework I play with my friends. We play football. I like football and my friends like football too. We play football in the park near my house. The park is near my house and it is a big park. We play football for one hour or sometimes two hours. Football is my favorite sport. I play football every day after school except Friday. On Friday I go to English class. I go to English class on the Friday because I want to learn English. English is important and I want to learn English.

In the evening I eat dinner with my family. We eat dinner at eight o'clock. After dinner I watch TV or I play on my phone. I like to watch TV and I like to play on my phone. Sometimes I am study for the tests but not very much. Then I go to bed at ten o'clock. I go to bed at ten o'clock because I must wake up early for school.

This is my school and this is what I do after school. My school is good and my after school is good too. I hope you like my email. Please write me and tell me about your school and about what you do after school. I want to know about your school and about what you do after school.

Best wishes,
Karim

task: Your school is holding a Volunteering Week and the student council wants more students to take part. Write a text for students aged 15-18 to persuade them to give some of their free time to help in the local community. Choose one: a speech for the school assembly, a blog post for the school website, or an article for the school magazine.
text:
Good morning, everyone, and thank you for putting down your phones for the next three minutes. I promise it will be worth it.

Let me begin with a simple question. When was the last time you did something that mattered to someone you will never see again? Not a message, not a like, not a joke in the group chat. I mean something real: an hour of your time that made a stranger's day slightly easier.

If you cannot remember, you are not alone. I could not either, until last spring, when I gave up two Saturday mornings to help at the Maple Street food bank. I went because a teacher mentioned that it would look good on my university application. I stayed because of Mrs Alvarez. She was seventy-three, she came every week to collect a bag of groceries, and she told me, while I was stacking tins of tomatoes, that our conversation was the first time anyone had asked about her life in a month. A month! That is longer than our last exam period.

I know what some of you are thinking. "I do not have the time." And honestly, I understand. Between deadlines, sports and, let us be honest, sleeping until noon, our weeks are packed. But think about how many hours we lose scrolling without even noticing. Two hours a month, the length of one film, is all that Volunteering Week asks of you. Ask yourself which of those two hours you will still remember in ten years.

Others will say that one person cannot change anything, that the problems of our city are too big for a teenager. I used to think so too. But look at what happened last year when only forty of us took part. We collected three hundred kilograms of food, painted the fence of the primary school and, perhaps most importantly, proved to the town council that our generation is more than a screen with legs. Small actions multiply when many people repeat them.

And here is something nobody tells you. Volunteering is not only a gift to others; it is a gift to yourself. You learn to listen, to organise, to work with people who do not share your opinions or even your language. These are the skills that no textbook can give and no employer can ignore. Surely that is a bargain: you give two hours and you receive a lifetime of confidence.

So what am I asking? Check the sign-up sheets outside the cafeteria. There are twelve projects, from reading with younger children to cleaning the river path. Choose one that sounds interesting, or even slightly frightening. Bring a friend if you need courage.

Because in the end, the question is not "Can I afford to give my time?" The question is "Can we afford not to?" Our town is not going to improve by itself; it is waiting for us.

Thank you. Now, who is brave enough to be the first to sign up?

task: Your school is holding a Volunteering Week and the student council wants more students to take part. Write a text for students aged 15-18 to persuade them to give some of their free time to help in the local community. Choose one: a speech for the school assembly, a blog post for the school website, or an article for the school magazine.
text:
Why You Should Volunteer This Month

Hi everyone! My name is Sara and I'm in the student council. Today I want to talk to you about something important: the Volunteering Week that is coming next month. I hope that after reading this blog you will decide to join us.

First of all, many students think that volunteering is boring or that is only for old people. But this is not true. Last year I helped in an animal shelter and I had a lot of fun. I walked dogs, cleaned the cages and played with the cats. At first I was nervous, but the people there were very kind and I made new friends. Now I go there every second Saturday.

Also, volunteering is good for your future. Universities and employers like to see that you did something useful in your free time. For example, my brother wrote about his volunteer work in his application and he got a place at a good university. So it is not only helping other people, it is also helping yourself.

Some students say they don't have enough time because of homework and exams. I understand this, because I also have many tests. However, you don't need to give much time. Just two or three hours is enough. You can choose a project which fits with your schedule, like reading to children after school or cleaning the beach on Sunday. In my opinion, it is a good way to relax from stress too.

Another reason is that it makes our community better. If every student help a little bit, the city will be cleaner and more people will be happy. Imagine how many old people are lonely at home, and a short visit from you can change their day.

So, what you need to do? It is very easy. Go to the school website and find the list of projects, then write your name. If you are shy, you can go with a friend. I promise you will not regret it!

Let's make this Volunteering Week the best one ever. Thank you for reading and see you at the projects!

Sara

task: Your school is holding a Volunteering Week. Write a speech to be delivered to your classmates at the school assembly, persuading them (aged 15-18) to give some of their free time to help in the local community.
text:
The Case for Student Volunteering

Volunteering among adolescents has been the subject of considerable debate in recent years. While critics argue that the pressures of modern schooling leave little room for unpaid work, there is substantial evidence that participation in community service benefits both the individual and society. This essay will examine three principal arguments in favour of student volunteering and consider one common objection.

The first argument concerns personal development. Research conducted in several countries suggests that young people who volunteer regularly develop stronger communication skills, greater empathy and a clearer sense of purpose. Working alongside people from different backgrounds, for example, requires a degree of patience and adaptability that the classroom rarely demands. It could therefore be argued that volunteering complements formal education rather than competing with it.

Secondly, volunteering generates tangible benefits for the community. Local food banks, care homes and environmental projects often depend on unpaid helpers, and a modest contribution from a large group of students can make a considerable difference. A school of one thousand pupils, each donating two hours a month, would provide two thousand hours of assistance, the equivalent of a full-time worker for an entire year.

Thirdly, there is the question of long-term civic engagement. Studies indicate that individuals who volunteer in adolescence are significantly more likely to remain active citizens in adulthood. Consequently, schools that encourage volunteering may be investing in a more cohesive society.

The most common objection is that students simply lack the time. This is a legitimate concern, particularly during examination periods. Nevertheless, the commitment required is small, and many projects can be scheduled flexibly. Moreover, it is worth noting that the time spent on social media by the average teenager greatly exceeds the hours that would be necessary.

In conclusion, the evidence suggests that student volunteering is beneficial on several levels. Although the practical obstacles should not be ignored, they are far from insurmountable. Schools should therefore continue to promote initiatives such as Volunteering Week, and students would be well advised to take part.
